questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: Genre and period before a question can be asked
questions.learningObjective: Identify the information that must be fixed before a question about a poem can be framed.
questions.stem: Before asking why a poem's closing line repeats a word used only in its title, the log-keeper first checks what kind of book the poem came from.

options.text: the author's reputation, since a writer's standing tells a reader what to expect of the poem
options.misconception: believes a writer's standing fixes what a poem means

options.text: the publisher's marketing copy, because sales language frames how most readers approach a book
options.misconception: treats marketing copy as evidence of a book's period

options.text: the genre and period of the poem, which set the expectations the poem answers or frustrates
the length of the poem, since form and lineation reveal a period more exactly than a label
options.misconception: confuses the poem's length with its historical moment

questions.explanation: Genre and period fix the expectations a text inherits before any line is examined. Reputation and marketing describe reception, not the text's situation, and length says nothing about when it was written.
questions.hint: Ask what the text was written to do.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: Two expectations, two forms, two conclusions
questions.learningObjective: Explain how two forms shape the conclusions a reader can draw from one event.

stimulus.body: Entry for 3 November: read the two comedies back to back this week. The first restores the household before the last page. The second names the culprits and leaves them standing in the yard. Same household, same debt, opposite closings. Writing down which shape each ending belongs to before deciding which one I actually prefer.

questions.stem: A reader comparing two comedies notices that one ends in reconciliation and the other ends in exposure, and asks which ending their forms make possible.

options.text: Each ending suits its own form, so judging both by one standard hides the real difference
The reconciling comedy is better because reconciliation is the older convention and so the truer form
options.misconception: assumes an older convention is the truer form

options.text: The exposing comedy is better because a comedy that resolves proves less than one that leaves things open
options.misconception: judges a comedy by how little it resolves

options.text: Both endings are equally strong, so the comparison should be dropped as a matter of taste
options.misconception: treats equal enjoyment as the end of analysis

questions.explanation: Each form carries its own expectations about how a story may close. Measuring one comedy by the other's habit mistakes a difference of form for a difference in quality.
questions.hint: Ask what each ending does to the world of the play.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: What two translations of one word disclose
questions.learningObjective: Explain what two renderings of one word disclose about the source word.
questions.stem: Two translators render the same compound word differently, and the log-keeper wants to explain what their renderings disclose about the source.

answer.exemplar: Each rendering shows a translator's decision about what the word does in its own sentence. One keeps the concrete sense and the other the moral weight, so the pair reveals that the term carried both at once, and that any single English word must lose whichever half the translator chose not to keep.

questions.explanation: Two renderings of one word expose the choices a translator made and the pressure the original word exerted. Where the renderings diverge, the source term was carrying more than one sense at once.
questions.hint: Look at what each translator chose to keep.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: Two renderings of one title
questions.learningObjective: Evaluate two renderings of one title by the promise the text keeps.
questions.stem: Two renderings of one title are compared, and the log entry asks which rendering better carries the promise the book then keeps.

options.text: The plainer title, because a title should name the subject plainly and leave its art to the pages
options.misconception: assumes a title must name the subject plainly

options.text: The stranger title, because a striking opening phrase pulls a reader further into an unfamiliar book
options.misconception: values a title for attention rather than accuracy

options.text: Neither, because titles are labels chosen by publishers and carry no authorial intent at all
options.misconception: denies titles any authorial intention

options.text: Whichever title keeps the promise of the book, judged by what the text actually does in the opening

questions.explanation: A title makes a promise, and a rendering is judged by the promise the text then keeps. Plainness and novelty are only means; the text's actual behaviour is the test.
questions.hint: Read the opening pages before choosing.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: Two adaptations holding one element constant
questions.learningObjective: Explain what a shared element reveals when two versions hold it constant.
questions.stem: Two adaptations keep the same confession scene, and the log asks what the shared element reveals when the surrounding periods differ.

options.text: That the shared scene proves the period, not the author, determines what a story can confess
options.misconception: credits the period instead of the author with the confession

options.text: That holding one element constant lets a reader see what the changed setting adds or costs
That the shared scene shows the original version is authentic and the rest are only copies
options.misconception: treats the earliest version as the authentic one

options.text: That the shared scene proves the two versions belong to one lineage with no real difference
options.misconception: assumes one lineage with no meaningful difference

questions.explanation: Keeping one element constant turns two texts into a controlled pair, so differences can be attributed to the changed surroundings. The shared scene proves neither authorship nor a single lineage.
questions.hint: Think of it as one variable held steady.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: Four versions ranked by distance from a source
questions.learningObjective: Rank versions by distance from a source rather than by age or reputation.
questions.stem: The observer sorts four printed versions of a tale by how far each has moved from the earliest manuscript it can trace.

options.text: The version closest to the manuscript, since printing fixes a text and later copies only blur it
options.misconception: assumes printing stabilises a text and copies blur it

options.text: The version most widely read, because a text's influence is measured by the number of copies in circulation
options.misconception: measures textual distance by circulation rather than change

options.text: The version translated earliest, because translation shows when a work first found a new audience
options.misconception: treats the earliest translation as the truest witness

options.text: The version whose changes best explain the gaps in the manuscript, since distance means change

questions.explanation: Distance is measured by what a version changes and why, so gaps in the manuscript reveal the source's condition. Circulation, translation, and print record a version's history, not its distance.
questions.hint: Ask what each edition actually changed.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: What makes two narrators comparable
questions.learningObjective: Identify what makes two narrators comparable.

stimulus.body: Entry for 22 August: I keep hearing that the narrator of the sea romance and the narrator of the household memoir can be set side by side because both say 'I'. That is the whole argument so far. Both speak in the first person, and one of them is not a sailor at all. Maybe the pairing is about the telling rather than the life.

questions.stem: Two first-person narrators are said to be comparable, and the log asks what must be true before that comparison holds.

options.text: That both narrators tell their own story in the first person, and that their voices are distinct
That both narrators have travelled widely and can therefore speak for a whole class of people
options.misconception: assumes wide travel alone makes a narrator representative

options.text: That both narrators are unreliable, since only a doubtful teller invites a comparison with another
options.misconception: assumes unreliability is the price of first-person telling

options.text: That both narrators come from the same country, so a shared background supplies shared meaning
options.misconception: believes a shared homeland settles what a voice means

questions.explanation: Two narrators are comparable when both tell their own story and each voice is distinct enough to examine. Travel, unreliability, and birthplace are separate claims that do not follow from the pronoun.
questions.hint: Separate the pronoun from the person.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: Genre and period before a question can be asked
questions.learningObjective: Explain why genre and period precede the framing of a question.
questions.stem: An entry from 14 October explains why genre and period must be settled before a question about a text can be framed.

answer.exemplar: A question about what a poem is doing depends on what kind of poem it is and when it was written, because both set the expectations the text answers, resists, or parodies. Fixing the kind and the date first turns a vague worry into a question that can be answered, and stops the reader from measuring a text by conventions it never accepted.

questions.explanation: Genre and period supply the expectations a text answers or resists. Naming them first turns vague unease into a question the text can settle, and prevents judging by conventions the work never accepted.
questions.hint: Ask what the work was expected to do.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: Two expectations, two forms, two conclusions
questions.learningObjective: Explain how two ballads' forms make a shared line promise different things.
questions.stem: Two ballads share an opening line, and the log asks what each form makes that line promise and deliver.

options.text: The line means the same in both, since a shared opening must carry the same traditional meaning
options.misconception: assumes a shared line carries one traditional meaning

options.text: Each ballad's form makes a different promise, so the shared line works in different directions
The line is a formulaic borrowing, and formulas carry no meaning of their own at all
options.misconception: believes formulaic phrases carry no meaning at all

options.text: The line proves the later ballad is the older one, since traditional phrasing cannot be invented twice
options.misconception: reads a shared formula as proof of which ballad came first

questions.explanation: Ballads sharing a line may belong to different traditions with different obligations, so the same words can promise a lament in one and a boast in another. Formulaic phrasing neither fixes meaning nor dates a text.
questions.hint: Consider what each ballad tradition promises.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: What two translations of one word disclose
questions.learningObjective: Explain what the divergence between two renderings discloses.
questions.stem: A translator's note records two renderings of a single word and asks what the difference between them discloses.

options.text: Only that one translator read the passage more carefully than the other one did
options.misconception: reads the difference as a difference in translator care

options.text: Only that the second rendering was chosen because it is easier for English readers to pronounce
options.misconception: explains the choice by ease of pronunciation for readers

options.text: That the original word carried two senses at once, each translation preserving one of them
That the original word was ambiguous only because the translators lacked a shared source text
options.misconception: blames translator access to the source for the divergence

questions.explanation: When two renderings of one word diverge, the source word was doing two jobs and each translation kept one. The note documents the pressure of the original, not either translator's care or convenience.
questions.hint: Ask which sense each rendering keeps.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: Genre and period before a question can be asked
questions.learningObjective: Identify what must be fixed before two novels of different kinds are compared.
questions.stem: One novel is a picaresque chronicle and the other is a novel of manners, and the log asks what must be fixed before they are compared at all.

options.text: The century in which each was published, since the two forms belong to different national literatures
options.misconception: fixes the comparison on national origin, not literary kind

options.text: The reading public each was written for, since the two forms answer different readers' expectations
options.misconception: takes the reading public as the only thing worth fixing

options.text: The size of each book, since long books and short books belong to different genres by necessity
options.misconception: believes book length determines genre

options.text: The genre and period of each, because a picaresque chronicle and a novel of manners make different promises

questions.explanation: Fix the genre and period that set each work's expectations before comparing, since a picaresque chronicle and a novel of manners answer different promises. National origin and length are context only.
questions.hint: Kind and date come before comparison.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: Two expectations, two forms, two conclusions
questions.learningObjective: Compare the conclusions a tragedy and a chronicle play can each reach.

stimulus.body: Entry for 9 July: the same defeat appears in two plays I read this month. In the tragedy a general falls and the city is left to argue about the corpse. In the chronicle the general is recorded, the campaign is summarised, and the next entry begins. Reading them together I want to know what each shape lets a reader conclude about that loss.

questions.stem: A reader comparing a tragedy and a chronicle play asks which conclusions each form makes available about a single defeat.

options.text: The tragedy settles the defeat's meaning, while the chronicle only records what happened afterwards
options.misconception: gives the tragedy sole power to fix what the defeat means

options.text: The tragedy can show the loss as a catastrophe, while the chronicle must treat it as one entry among many
Neither play concludes anything, since dramatic endings are always a matter of a director's staging
options.misconception: believes conclusions belong to staging rather than to form

options.text: Both plays reach the same conclusion, because the two genres were built for identical moral purposes
options.misconception: assumes two genres were built for the same moral purpose

questions.explanation: A tragedy can make a defeat a catastrophe by concentrating everything on it, while a chronicle must place the loss among other events. Neither is more truthful; each is a different shape of conclusion.
questions.hint: Ask what each form can make of one event.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: What two translations of one word disclose
questions.learningObjective: Explain what a verse rendering and a prose gloss reveal together.
questions.stem: The log-keeper notes that a single word is rendered one way in verse and quite another in a gloss written later.

options.text: The prose rendering is truer, because a gloss is free of the constraints that shaped the original line
options.misconception: assumes the unconstrained prose gloss is the truer witness

options.text: Each rendering answers a different purpose, so the pair shows what each context could not hold
The verse rendering is truer, because poetic diction is older and therefore closer to the first usage
options.misconception: assumes older diction is automatically more accurate

options.text: Neither rendering can be checked, because word choice in a translation admits no external test
options.misconception: believes translation choices resist any check at all

questions.explanation: A verse line and a later prose gloss do different work, so their renderings diverge for a reason. The pair shows what each context could not carry, rather than ranking one as true.
questions.hint: Ask what each context needed the word to do.

questions.topic: Two renderings of one title
questions.learningObjective: Evaluate two renderings of one play title by the text's own promise.
questions.stem: A play carries one title on its title page and another in the programme, and the entry asks which better keeps the promise of the text.

options.text: The title page, because a printed title is fixed at printing and cannot be revised to flatter
options.misconception: trusts the printed title because it cannot be revised

options.text: The programme title, because a later edition has had longer to discover what the play is about
options.misconception: assumes later editions know the play better

options.text: Neither, because a title promises a subject and plays never keep their subjects
options.misconception: denies that a play could keep a promise at all

options.text: Whichever the text keeps, judged by the first act rather than by the printing history

questions.explanation: A title makes a promise, so the promise is tested against what the play does, beginning in the first act. Printing history shows how a text was handled, not what it delivers.
questions.hint: Read the first act before judging.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: Two adaptations holding one element constant
questions.learningObjective: Explain what a comparison of two versions with one constant can establish.
questions.stem: A short story and a filmed adaptation keep the same flood scene, and the log asks what the comparison can and cannot establish.

options.text: The shared flood scene isolates what each medium adds, without proving one version explains the other
The shared flood scene proves the film is a faithful record of what the story actually meant
options.misconception: reads the shared scene as proof of the film's faithfulness

options.text: The shared flood scene proves the earlier story was written to be filmed, since the two are too alike
options.misconception: infers the earlier work was written with filming in mind

options.text: The shared flood scene proves nothing at all, since adaptation and original share no material
options.misconception: denies any useful comparison between the two versions

questions.explanation: Holding the flood scene constant turns the pair into a comparison of mediums, revealing what film adds and what the story alone can do. It establishes neither a direction of influence nor the meaning of the original.
questions.hint: One constant, two mediums, one question.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: Four versions ranked by distance from a source
questions.learningObjective: Explain how versions are ranked by distance from an earliest state.
questions.stem: Four printed versions of the same letter are ranked by their distance from the source, and the log explains how that ranking is made.

answer.exemplar: The ranking is made by comparing each printing with the surviving copies of the letter's earliest state and noting which differences can be explained as slips or corrections and which cannot. A version that agrees with the earliest state in everything but a single explained slip sits nearer the source than one whose differences are numerous and unaccounted for.

questions.explanation: Ranking measures each version against the earliest recoverable state and asks whether its differences are explained. Distance is a claim about change and cause, not about age or popularity.
questions.hint: Judge change, not age or popularity.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: What makes two narrators comparable
questions.learningObjective: Identify what makes two narrators comparable enough for pairing.
questions.stem: A scholar compares a journal entry with a published memoir and asks what makes the two narrators comparable enough for the pairing.

options.text: That both narrators describe the same stretch of time, since subject matter is what links two accounts
options.misconception: grounds comparability in shared subject matter rather than voice

options.text: That both appear in the same set of margins, since a shared frame of reference guarantees comparability
options.misconception: assumes a shared frame makes any two voices comparable

options.text: That each voice has its own way of telling, so the telling itself can be examined side by side
That both narrators end their accounts in the same year, since a shared endpoint makes them comparable
options.misconception: grounds comparability in a shared ending rather than in the voices

questions.explanation: Two narrators become comparable when their ways of telling can be examined together, which needs distinct voices rather than shared subjects or dates. A journal entry and a memoir also differ in audience and purpose.
questions.hint: Look for the voice, not the subject.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: Genre and period before a question can be asked
questions.learningObjective: Identify what must be established before two poems are grouped as satire.

stimulus.body: Entry for 5 May: I nearly filed two poems together as satire because both end in a sneer. Then I checked the pages and found one printed in a pamphlet sold at a fair and the other posted on a wall in a college yard. The joke is the same in each, and the danger aimed at it is not the same at all.

questions.stem: Before grouping two poems as satire, the log insists on fixing what each poem belongs to and when it appeared.

options.text: Their tone settles the matter, since a sneering ending marks satire in any setting
options.misconception: takes a sneering tone as proof of satirical kind

options.text: Their subject settles it, since satire is judged by what it takes aim at
options.misconception: believes the target alone determines a text's genre

options.text: Their length settles it, since shorter poems are usually the more satirical
options.misconception: reads brevity as a reliable sign of satirical purpose

options.text: The kind of publication and its audience settle it, since satire aims at what its readers recognise

questions.explanation: Satire points at something its readers already know, so the setting of publication and the assumed audience matter before any grouping. Tone and length can look shared while the joke lands elsewhere.
questions.hint: Ask who could recognise the target.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: What two translations of one word disclose
questions.learningObjective: Analyse how a word's position changes its force in two lyrics.
questions.stem: The word 'harvest' closes one lyric and opens another, and the entry asks what the shared word does in each position.

options.text: The same in both, since a closing word sets a final tone and an opening word only announces a topic
options.misconception: believes a closing and an opening word carry identical force

options.text: Different in each, because a word at the close settles a reading while a word at the start opens one
Different in each, but only because one lyric is older and the other was written for a new fashion
options.misconception: credits fashion rather than position for the difference in force

options.text: The same in both, since the two lyricists plainly shared a single dictionary and a single taste
options.misconception: assumes shared vocabulary guarantees a shared effect

questions.explanation: Position changes what a word can do: at a close it settles the reading a poem has built, at an opening it proposes one. The shared word shows two mechanisms, and a shared dictionary explains neither.
questions.hint: Read the same word at two different ends.

questions.topic: Two renderings of one title
questions.learningObjective: Explain what comparing two titles of one book can and cannot establish.
questions.stem: A publisher reissued a chapbook with a new title, and the log asks what a comparison of the two titles can establish.

options.text: That the old title was inadequate, since a publisher reissues books precisely to correct bad titles
options.misconception: treats reissue as proof the earlier title was faulty

options.text: That the new title sells better, since reissued titles are chosen for their power in the market
options.misconception: explains the change by commercial calculation alone

options.text: That the two titles promise different readings of the same book, and only the text says which it keeps
That the two titles are interchangeable, since the contents of a book do not depend on how it is announced
options.misconception: assumes a title has no power over how a book is read

questions.explanation: A title sets an expectation, so a reissued title opens a second reading of the same text. The comparison shows two promises were made; only the text shows which one the book keeps.
questions.hint: Titles promise; the text delivers.

questions.topic: Two adaptations holding one element constant
questions.learningObjective: Explain what a constant element lets a reader test in two adaptations.
questions.stem: Two stage adaptations keep the same final scene, and the log asks what that constant lets a reader test.

options.text: Whether the two versions share a single original, since an identical scene cannot be invented twice
options.misconception: assumes an identical scene proves a single original

options.text: Whether the changed surroundings strengthen or weaken the scene, since everything else now varies
Whether one adaptation is the better play, since a shared scene offers a fair test of quality
options.misconception: reads the fixed scene as a fair test of overall quality

options.text: Whether audiences prefer endings, since a fixed scene isolates the audience's response
options.misconception: takes the control as a way to measure audience taste

questions.explanation: A constant scene turns the pair into a test of surroundings, so the reader can see what the changed setting does to it. It does not prove a single original, rank overall quality, or isolate audience taste.
questions.hint: Everything else is now variable.

questions.topic: Four versions ranked by distance from a source
questions.learningObjective: Evaluate whether plainness of manner can rank a version's distance.
questions.stem: Four versions of an elegy are ranked, and the log asks whether plainness of manner counts as evidence of distance from the source.

options.text: It does, because plainness of manner marks a period as surely as any dated reference
options.misconception: treats plainness of manner as decisive evidence of distance

options.text: It does, because a plain style is characteristic of versions copied in the eighteenth century
options.misconception: assumes plain style belongs only to earlier copies

options.text: It does, because only a copy made in a settled period can write in an unadorned manner
options.misconception: believes plain writing signals a settled historical moment

options.text: It does not by itself, because plainness is available in every period and needs other evidence

questions.explanation: Plainness of manner is available in every period, so it cannot by itself rank a version's distance from a source. Dated references, patronage, and print practice carry the weight instead, since style drifts.
questions.hint: Style alone does not rank a text.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: What makes two narrators comparable
questions.learningObjective: Identify what makes two narrators comparable.

stimulus.body: Entry for 24 February: the two accounts I mean are a steward's tally and a traveller's tale. Both say 'I', and that is the whole argument for setting them beside each other. One counts sacks and never leaves the yard; the other crosses three mountains and admits nothing about what he saw. Perhaps the pairing should be about how each of them tells, rather than what each of them was in.

questions.stem: Two narrators are said to be comparable because both speak in the first person, and the log asks what else that comparison requires.

options.text: That each voice has its own way of reporting, since comparison needs two tellings that can be examined
That both narrators are written in the first person, since the pronoun alone establishes comparability
options.misconception: believes a shared pronoun alone makes narrators comparable

options.text: That both narrators travel, since a journey is the common ground a reader can rely on
options.misconception: assumes a shared journey supplies comparability

options.text: That one narrator is the more reliable, since a comparison must end by choosing between them
options.misconception: insists comparison must end in a verdict on reliability

questions.explanation: Two narrators become comparable when each voice has its own way of reporting, so the telling can be examined side by side. A shared pronoun, a shared journey, and a reliability verdict are other claims.
questions.hint: Compare the reporting, not the pronoun.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: Genre and period before a question can be asked
questions.learningObjective: Explain how a period shapes a reader's first expectations.
questions.stem: The log-keeper explains what a period does to a reader's first expectations of an unfamiliar play.

answer.exemplar: A period settles the horizon of what a reader may expect before the first line is read, because a play of that time inherited certain kinds of plot, certain stages, and certain kinds of joke. Knowing the period lets a reader judge an oddity as a deliberate departure rather than a mistake, and lets an apparent failure be read as the consequence of a convention the playwright chose.

questions.explanation: Period supplies inherited expectations about plot, staging, and tone, so knowing it lets a reader read an oddity as deliberate and a failure as a consequence of convention. Without it, deviations look like incompetence.
questions.hint: What was expected before the first line?

questions.topic: Two expectations, two forms, two conclusions
questions.learningObjective: Frame a question that two forms of different kinds can both answer.
questions.stem: A reader wants to know whether a revenge tragedy and a domestic novel can support the same conclusion about justice.

options.text: Only the revenge tragedy can, because moral conclusions belong to plays and not to novels
options.misconception: restricts moral judgement to dramatic forms

options.text: Only the domestic novel can, because novels show consequence and plays only display intention
options.misconception: restricts moral judgement to narrative prose

options.text: Only if the question is framed so that each form's expectations shape the answer it can reach
Yes, automatically, because both forms end with a penalty that the audience is meant to accept
options.misconception: assumes a shared penalty guarantees a shared conclusion

questions.explanation: The two forms reach conclusions of different kinds, so a shared question must be framed so each answer matches what that form can supply. A common penalty is not a common conclusion.
questions.hint: Frame the question to fit each form.

questions.stem: Two translations render a word for a bird, and the log asks what a comparison of the renderings can show about the source.

options.text: That the original word named a bird by its sound, its shape, or its habit, and each version kept one
That the first translator knew the word better, since the second version is far more common
options.misconception: ranks translators by how usual their chosen word is

options.text: That the bird was a domestic one, because translators pick only birds their readers keep
options.misconception: infers the bird's habits from translators' choices

options.text: That the two renderings are unrelated, since no single original word could mean both
options.misconception: insists a single source word can carry only one sense

questions.explanation: When two renderings of a bird's name diverge, the original fixed the bird by one feature and each version kept one. How usual a word is, and what the bird's life was like, are side matters.
questions.hint: Ask what feature the original named.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: Two renderings of one title
questions.learningObjective: Evaluate two renderings of one title against the book's opening pages.

stimulus.body: Entry for 11 January: the pamphlet carries one title in print and another in the catalogue entry that the bookseller wrote. The catalogue version promises a lesson for the young. The printed title promises a warning. I read the first three pages twice before deciding which promise the book actually keeps, and it is not the one either title states plainly.

questions.stem: A pamphlet carries one title in print and another in the catalogue, and the log asks which one the opening pages support.

options.text: The catalogue version, because a bookseller's entry reports the book better than a title does
options.misconception: trusts a bookseller's description over the book's own pages

options.text: Neither title alone, since the opening pages show a third expectation the two titles missed
The printed title, because a title printed on the page is the author's own final choice of words
options.misconception: assumes the printed title must be the author's final intention

options.text: Both equally, since a title is only a label and carries no promise a reader need trust
options.misconception: denies that a title sets any expectation on a reader

questions.explanation: The opening pages show what the book keeps, and here they support a third expectation neither title states. A catalogue description, a printed title, and the claim that titles are empty labels all miss it.
questions.hint: Let the first three pages decide.

options.misconception: believes a fixed object always carries a fixed symbolism

options.misconception: dates the works by how early the motif appears in print

options.text: That the motif means different work in each, since its force depends on what surrounds it

questions.explanation: A motif carries whatever weight its surroundings give it, so the lamp in a drama and in a radio play need not do the same work. Particularity does not prove borrowing, and symbolism is not fixed.

options.text: That both works describe the same trade route, since shared subject matter proves shared concerns
options.misconception: grounds the pairing in shared subject matter alone

options.text: That the memoir is the more reliable account, since a traveller's duty is to report what he saw
options.misconception: treats a stated duty to report as a guarantee of accuracy

options.text: That the two works belong to one tradition of adventure, since both send a reader on a journey
options.misconception: reduces both works to one tradition of adventure

options.text: That their two ways of telling can be compared, since each voice shapes what its journey becomes

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: Genre and period before a question can be asked
questions.learningObjective: Identify what must be fixed before an allusion can be tested.

stimulus.body: Entry for 2 August: the line in question mentions a gate and a traveller stopped at it, and I keep wondering whether that is a nod to an older poem or just the sort of thing a lyricist reaches for. Before I put it in a notebook as a source, I should probably work out what kind of poem this is and how old it is.

questions.stem: A reader wants to test whether a line in a poem is a deliberate allusion or an ordinary turn of phrase.

options.text: Fix the poem's kind and date first, then check the phrase against what its period borrowed from
Check the line for rhymes, since a rhyme with an older poem settles the borrower's intention
options.misconception: believes a shared rhyme proves a deliberate borrowing

options.text: Look for a date printed on the copy, since an allusion matters only when the text is old
options.misconception: assumes only old texts contain allusions worth naming

options.text: Compare it with a translation of the same idea, since translators preserve borrowings that poets drop
options.misconception: treats translation as a better witness to allusion than the poem

questions.explanation: An allusion is judged against the borrowings a period was likely to make, so the poem's kind and date come first. Rhymes, the age of a copy, and a translator's choices are weaker evidence for intention.
questions.hint: Date the poem before chasing sources.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: Two expectations, two forms, two conclusions
questions.learningObjective: Explain why one subject yields two conclusions in two forms.
questions.stem: A note from 19 June explains why two forms built on the same subject produce two different conclusions about it.

answer.exemplar: A subject does not determine the conclusion a form will reach, because each form has its own shape of resolution. The verse drama must close its action within the limits of stage time, so it ends with the catastrophe that its structure has been preparing. The novel, which can postpone and interrupt, ends by showing what the action has cost the people inside it. The same material, two architectures, two endings.

questions.explanation: A form's shape of resolution decides the conclusion it can reach, so the same material ends differently in a stage drama and a novel. Stage time, interruption, and postponement are structural facts, not taste.
questions.hint: Ask how each form can end at all.

options.text: Only the metre, since a monosyllable can be fitted into any line the translator chooses to write
options.misconception: reduces the difference to a question of metrical convenience

options.text: Only the period of the two poems, since the word has always carried a single meaning everywhere
options.misconception: believes a word has carried one meaning in every period

options.text: The sense each poem gives the word, since the same term can stand for different things in different poems
Nothing at all, since translation is a matter of taste and no comparison of renderings is meaningful
options.misconception: denies that renderings can be compared at all

questions.explanation: The same word in two poems can carry different senses, and the renderings differ because the poems use it differently. Metre and period explain the handling of the line, not the sense.
questions.hint: Read the two poems, not just the words.

options.misconception: judges a title by its sound before its accuracy

options.text: The one printed first, since the original title was chosen with the whole collection in view

questions.topic: Genre and period before a question can be asked
questions.learningObjective: Explain why a readership must be fixed before poems are grouped.
questions.stem: The log-keeper works out why a question about a periodical's readership must be settled before the poems in it are grouped.

answer.exemplar: Poems printed for a readership share a set of assumptions about what can be said without explanation, and those assumptions belong to the readership rather than to the poems themselves. Fixing who was meant to read the pages tells a reader what a poem could leave unsaid, and turns a guess about grouping into a question with a checkable answer.

questions.explanation: A readership supplies shared assumptions about what can be left unsaid, so it must be fixed before poems are grouped by what they assume. The poems then show what that audience took for granted.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: Two expectations, two forms, two conclusions
questions.learningObjective: Compare what two settings allow two endings to settle.

stimulus.body: Entry for 16 December: both comedies end with a proposal that is refused. In one, the refusal closes a legal argument and nothing more. In the other, the refusal sends the household out into the night and the last scene is spent on who carries the lamp. Different closures, same event, and I keep wanting to say the second is sadder without saying why.

questions.stem: Two comedies with different settings are compared, and the log asks what each setting allows the ending to do.

options.text: Nothing distinguishes them, since a refused proposal is a refused proposal wherever it happens
options.misconception: treats the shared event as making the two endings identical

options.text: The setting lets each refusal settle a different order of things, so the closings are not the same event
Only the last scene matters, since the final minutes of a comedy tell a reader what the evening meant
options.misconception: judges a comedy by its final scene alone

options.text: Only the legal argument matters, since a closed argument is more serious than a lamp in the rain
options.misconception: prefers a legal argument to a scene with a lamp in it

questions.explanation: Each setting lets the same event settle a different order of things, so the closings differ even though the proposal is refused twice. The final scene and the legal argument are each part of one ending.
questions.hint: Compare what each ending puts in order.

That the pair is accidental, since a shared source word rarely survives translation twice

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: Two adaptations holding one element constant
questions.learningObjective: Explain what becomes visible when one element is held fixed.
questions.stem: An entry from 3 March explains what becomes visible when two adaptations keep one element unchanged.

answer.exemplar: When two adaptations keep the same element unchanged, the element stops being a description of either work and becomes a test applied to both. The reader can then ask what each version does with the scene it inherited: what it adds, what it explains, what it leaves cold. Without the constant, the two versions simply differ, and the difference says nothing about which element is doing the work.

questions.explanation: A held constant becomes a test rather than a description, showing what each version does with the element it inherited. Without that control the versions merely differ, and difference shows nothing about where the work lies.
questions.hint: One fixed element becomes a test.

questions.topic: Two expectations, two forms, two conclusions
questions.learningObjective: Explain how different audiences produce different conclusions.
questions.stem: The entry for 27 October explains why the same event produces different conclusions in two forms with different audiences.

answer.exemplar: Two forms draw on the same event and reach different conclusions because each serves a different audience with different expectations about what a conclusion is for. The chronicle reader wants to know what followed, so the entry ends with the next appointment. questions.explanation: One verb can carry an active and a passive stance at once, and each rendering fixes one, so the pair discloses a word doing double work. Smoothness and misreading are surface explanations.

options.text: The second says more, because an ending in open water keeps the danger of the sea in front of the reader
options.misconception: rates an ending by whether the danger stays visible

options.text: They say the same thing, since every sea story ends by telling a reader whether the sea won
options.misconception: assumes both stories must deliver the same verdict

options.text: Each says something its own form can support, so the endings are better compared than ranked

questions.explanation: Each sea story can only conclude in the way its form allows, so the endings are better compared than ranked. Conquest, danger, and a shared verdict are readings one of the two forms cannot sustain.
questions.hint: Compare what each form can finish with.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: What two translations of one word disclose
questions.learningObjective: Analyse what a difference in dialect records about a narrator.
questions.stem: Two dialects of one word appear in the same poem, and the log asks what the difference between them records.

options.text: The social rank of the speakers, since dialect marks class and nothing else in a poem
options.misconception: reads dialect as a class label and nothing more

options.text: The distance the poet keeps from one voice, since a word's form shows how near a speaker is held
The date of the poem, since a dialect word belongs to one period and cannot cross into another
options.misconception: believes a dialect word cannot appear in a later period

options.text: The printer's habits, since regional spellings usually reflect the shop that set the type
options.misconception: attributes regional spelling to the printing house

questions.explanation: A dialect form shows how near a voice the poet holds, a claim about the writing rather than the speaker's class. Such words travel across periods, and printers' habits explain spelling, not choice.
questions.hint: Dialect can show distance, not just class.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: Two renderings of one title
questions.learningObjective: Explain what a new title does to a borrowed scene.
questions.stem: A radio play borrows a novel's storm and gives it a new title, and the log asks what the pair makes visible.

options.text: That the radio play is the truer storm, since a spoken text cannot hide what a novel conceals
options.misconception: prefers the broadcast's plainness to the novel's concealment

options.text: That the titles differ only in length, since a broadcast title must be shorter than a book's
options.misconception: reduces the title change to a matter of broadcast length

options.text: That a new title recruits a new audience, and the borrowed storm is read differently because of it
That the pair shows nothing, since a title and a medium are separate things entirely
options.misconception: denies any comparison between title and medium

questions.explanation: A new title recruits a new audience, and the borrowed storm is read under that expectation, so the pair shows meaning shifting with framing. Broadcast plainness and title length miss that shift.
questions.hint: Titles change who is listening.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: Two adaptations holding one element constant
questions.learningObjective: Explain how a fixed element changes what a comparison can show.
questions.stem: An entry from 4 June explains how holding one element fixed changes the conclusions a reader can draw.

answer.exemplar: Holding one element fixed turns a comparison into an argument, because the reader is no longer tracking many differences at once but one. If the two versions keep the same death scene, then whatever else differs, the question can be narrowed to what the changed world around that scene does to it: the inherited expectations it meets, the readers who receive it, and the weight the scene is asked to carry.

questions.explanation: A fixed element narrows the comparison to the effects of everything else, so the reader can test what the changed surroundings do to an inherited scene. Without the control, differences are too many to argue from.
questions.hint: One fixed scene, one testable question.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: Four versions ranked by distance from a source
questions.learningObjective: Explain what makes one version nearer a source than another.
questions.stem: Four printed copies of one tale are ranked, and the log asks what makes a version nearer the source than another.

options.text: Its differences can be accounted for as changes made for a reason the copy itself explains
Its text is older, since a copy printed earlier always stands closer to the first telling
options.misconception: assumes the earliest printing stands nearest the first telling

options.text: Its name is better remembered, since a version people still name must be the true one
options.misconception: believes continued naming proves a version's authenticity

options.text: It is printed more completely, since a fuller copy preserves more of the tale than a partial one
options.misconception: treats completeness as proof of closeness to a source

questions.explanation: A version stands nearer the source when its departures can be explained, since an explained change marks a decision rather than drift. Age, reputation, and completeness describe a copy's history, not its distance.
questions.hint: Explained change keeps a version near.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: What makes two narrators comparable
questions.learningObjective: Evaluate which comparison of two narrators yields knowledge.
questions.stem: A reader compares two narrators and asks which comparison of them will actually yield knowledge.

options.text: Comparing their incomes, since money shapes a narrator's chances more surely than tone does
options.misconception: believes circumstances outweigh a narrator's way of telling

options.text: Comparing their publications, since a shared publisher makes two voices comparable
options.misconception: assumes a shared publisher makes two voices comparable

options.text: Comparing their ways of organising what they saw, since arrangement is where a voice shows
Comparing their ages, since the older narrator has had longer to learn what the world is
options.misconception: measures a narrator's value by years of experience

questions.explanation: Arrangement shows a voice at work, so comparing how two narrators organise what they saw is where knowledge about them comes from. Circumstances, publishers, and age settle nothing about the telling.
questions.hint: Look at how each one orders events.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: Genre and period before a question can be asked
questions.learningObjective: Identify what must be fixed before two uses of a phrase are compared.

stimulus.body: Entry for 13 April: the same two words turn up in a satire about a town's eating habits and in a collection of prayers printed for country parishes. Before I write them down as the same phrase with the same sense, I should be able to say what kind of book each one is, because a joke and a petition are not the same sort of object.

questions.stem: A single phrase, 'bread and salt', appears in a satire and in a prayer book, and the log asks what must be fixed first.

options.text: The date of each printing, since a phrase can only mean one thing in any given century
options.misconception: believes a phrase is fixed by its century alone

options.text: The printer's name, since two printings from one shop share a house style
options.misconception: thinks a shared printer settles a shared sense

options.text: The kind of book each phrase appears in, since each belongs to a different set of uses
The number of copies printed, since a common phrase proves a common source for both
options.misconception: infers a shared source from a shared popular phrase

questions.explanation: A phrase belongs to the kind of work that uses it, so each book's genre must be fixed before senses are compared. A date, a printer, and a print run describe a book physically, not its use.
questions.hint: Fix the kind of book before the sense.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: Two expectations, two forms, two conclusions
questions.learningObjective: Explain what a shared subtitle and two forms together suggest.
questions.stem: Two books share a subtitle, and the log asks what their shared promise and their different forms together suggest.

options.text: That one promise can be carried by two forms, so the shared words set an aim rather than a result
That the subtitle belongs to whichever book came second, since publishers reuse what sells
options.misconception: assumes the later publisher copied the subtitle for profit

options.text: That the two books are the same work issued twice, since publishers do not coin new subtitles
options.misconception: treats a shared subtitle as proof of a duplicated work

options.text: That a subtitle promises nothing at all, since it is only a shelf label in smaller type
options.misconception: dismisses a subtitle as mere shelf labelling

questions.explanation: A shared subtitle sets one aim that two different forms may each pursue, so the words name a target rather than a result. Reuse for profit, duplicated work, and mere labelling each miss that purpose.
questions.hint: A shared promise, two different deliveries.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: What two translations of one word disclose
questions.learningObjective: Evaluate which difference between two renderings is worth recording.
questions.stem: Two translations of a poem's central word differ, and the log asks which difference is worth recording and why.

options.text: Only the one that changes the poem's length, since a translation should fit the original metre
options.misconception: prioritises metrical fit over the word's work in the poem

options.text: Only the one that alters the poem's tone, since tone matters more to a reader than sense
options.misconception: prioritises tone over the sense the poem asks for

options.text: Only the one the publisher preferred, since the published version is the one readers will meet
options.misconception: prioritises the publisher's choice over the translator's problem

options.text: The one that shifts what the poem asks of its reader, since the word's work in the whole changes

questions.explanation: The difference worth recording is the one that changes what the poem asks of its reader, since that is where a word's work lies. Metre, tone, and publisher preference are secondary.
questions.hint: Ask what the poem now demands of you.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: Two renderings of one title
questions.learningObjective: Explain what a comparison of two title renderings can and cannot settle.
questions.stem: The log compares two renderings of a play's title and explains what the comparison can and cannot settle.

answer.exemplar: Two renderings of one title can be compared for the promises they make and for how each one shapes the first hour of reading, which is a real difference and worth writing down. What the comparison cannot settle is which title the author would have chosen, since titles are made by publishers, printers, and friends as often as by writers, and the evidence for intention usually fails.

questions.explanation: Two titles can be compared for the promises they make and how each shapes a reading, which is a genuine difference. Authorial intention cannot be settled this way, since publishers, printers, and friends make titles too.
questions.hint: Compare promises, not intentions.
